claims.text: The initial material is an as-sintered VFeTiTaW high-entropy alloy.
The as-sintered alloy has a homogeneously distributed multi-element matrix.
Annealing VFeTiTaW at approximately 1000–1100 °C for 1–2 hours will produce controlled tungsten precipitation.
The tungsten precipitates will preferentially form at strategic locations such as grain boundaries.
Tungsten-rich precipitates will form continuous high-thermal-conductivity channels.
The remaining high-entropy matrix will retain phase stability and mechanical strength after precipitation.
Tungsten has inherently high thermal conductivity that can facilitate electron-mediated heat transfer in this microstructure.
Limiting phase segregation to tungsten will preserve the structural integrity supplied by the high-entropy matrix.
The annealed alloy will have higher effective thermal conductivity than the as-sintered alloy.
The annealed alloy will preserve, or only marginally reduce, mechanical integrity relative to the as-sintered alloy.
The proposed performance improvement will persist at operating temperatures of 1100–1300 °C.
The proposed performance improvement will persist under high thermal flux and irradiation representative of plasma-facing reactor service.
A thermal barrier interlayer is required between tungsten plasma-facing material and CuCrZr cooling pipes because of their different working temperatures.
The as-sintered VFeTiTaW alloy is a current intermediate layer in use between tungsten and CuCrZr components.
Long annealing or annealing at higher temperatures can cause increased phase growth in VFeTiTaW.
Excessive phase growth or coarsening will degrade both thermal and mechanical properties.
Variability in tungsten precipitate size and distribution may alter the balance between thermal enhancement and mechanical stability.
Prolonged irradiation may cause microstructural evolution that affects long-term thermal and mechanical performance.
